title: What is the biggest “What If?” story in movie history

commenti.body: Orson Welles' lost cut of The Magnificent Ambersons, and probably a hundred other stories related to projects he wanted to complete and/or stuff he shot that was cut/mismanaged by the studios.
[removed]

On a larger scale, the uncut Ambersons and Jodorowsky’s Dune come to mind, but for me, I always come back to Clint Eastwood, Eli Wallach, and Lee Van Cleef playing the three bad guys waiting for Charles Bronson at the start of Once Upon a Time in the West. From what I remember, Lee and Eli were willing but Eastwood wasn’t down and the idea fell apart. I think it’s a masterpiece as it is, but goddamn that would’ve been cool
[removed]
Imagine just giving that guy the proper damn funding

Always wonder about Darren Aronofsky and Joaquin Phoenix’s potential Batman: Year One (but v glad with how things turned out with Nolan).

Script is online - it’s gritty: https://archive.org/details/batman-year-one-frank-miller-script/page/n1/mode/1up

And nice read.

Probably what if Godfather Part IV got made if Mario Puzo lived longer. You can only imagine what it would've looked like to see the parallel storylines of the Corleone family's prime and Young Sonny's entry into the business, along with Don Vincent's reign and the eventual decline & end of the family.

Additionally, the possibility of having Leonardo DiCaprio in it alongside a returning Robert De Niro & Andy Garcia.

The biggest? What if Marilyn Monroe didn’t overdose. She was hardcore about studying the craft, continuing to train. It’s fascinating to think about how she would have coped with aging. If Hollywood would have banished her for not being the latest it girl anymore. Her devotion to acting is legendary. She really cared about studying! What if in her 60s and 70s and 80s she finally broke away from the sex symbol and found a new way to express?! 

Another tragedy is Faye Dunaway. What if she turned down Mommie Dearest? She never would have been blacklisted in Hollywood. I hate it when people judge her for that and say she wasn’t great. Network and Chinatown are masterpieces and Faye was brilliant in them. She’s a truly good actress. And she asked the director on Mommie Dearest to tell her if she was going too far. I think we lost out on a lot of great Faye performances because of that snafu.

Jessica Tandy. What if they chose her over Vivien Leigh? 

I wonder what if a lot. What if Dwayne Johnson and John Cena had the courage to go to acting studio, study hard, explore! Instead they just survive on popularity and hubris. Peter Dinklage. What if they put in the effort to do more acting training in a studio and with a good teacher?

Another tragedy? John Waters. Hollywood should let him keep making pictures. Not just hang out at the Baltimore bookstore all day. You wonder what else could come out of his mind.

Del Toro directing The Hobbit. Studio was in financial trouble delaying the film(s) resulting in Del Toro stepping away and PJ pulling a rabbit out of a hat, not the ideal vision the two had worked on for years.
Similarly, Peter Bogdanovich worked on a screenplay for The Streets of Laredo that he wrote with Henry Fonda, John Wayne, and Jimmy Stewart in mind.
[removed]
[removed]

These probably aren’t the biggest by any means but there’s a few that immediately jumped into my mind:

Kubrick’s Napoleon movie that was halted in pre production after the lack of box office success of Waterloo.

Nolan’s Howard Hughes biopic.

Iirc Johnathan Nolan was originally commissioned to write Interstellar for Stephen Spielberg. Eventually something fell through and Johnathan suggested to the studio that his brother direct it instead.

Would Django and the Matrix be viewed any differently if Will Smith hadn’t passed on the lead roles?

Brad Pitt apparently had a large bidding war with Scorsese/DiCaprio for the rights to make Wolf of Wall Street.

Nolan sold the Memento script but the studio didn’t trust him to direct it, that is before he drove to LA and put a copy of his first film on the doorstep of one of the studio’s executives.

It was rumored that OJ Simpson was in the running to star in the Terminator. Though James Cameron denies that he was ever considered.

Spielberg decided to keep the shark in Jaws hidden for the majority of the film because of technical difficulties with the robot shark that they’d built.

Scorsese had a big dispute about making changes to Taxi Driver so that it would get an R rating. The dispute was heated enough for him to apparently have seriously consider shooting someone involved over it.

Johnny Depp said in an interview that he had never considered acting until an actor friend told him he thought he’d be good at it and set him up with his agent.

Stephen Graham had only ever done TV stuff until his friend auditioned for Snatch where Guy Ritchie spotted Stephen outside waiting for his friend to finish and suggested that he audition for the part as well.

Iirc Coppola didn’t want to direct the Godfather.

Naomi Watts gave up on acting after shooting Mulholland Dr until the film released.

The head in the box ending of Se7en was originally shot down and changed by the studio. When Fincher signed on for the project the writer sent him the original script instead of the changed version and Fincher refused to do the movie if the head in the box ending was changed.

For years Scorsese has wanted to make a biopic of Frank Sinatra but the Sinatra estate won’t allow him to explore Frank’s mob ties.

The Coen Brothers couldn’t get Jeff Bridges to commit to making Lebowski so they wrote Fargo to shoot in the meantime instead.

Reservoir Dogs got made because Laurence Bender got the script to Harvey Keitel through a friend of his acting teacher’s wife.
[removed]

In that same vein, PJ and Neill Blomkamp's Halo project could have been what a Halo project actually needed instead of the fan film and paramount+'s underwhelming efforts we actually got. Emphasis on paramount+.

Not the biggest of course, but the one I care about the most is what if we actually got Sam Peckinpah’s true version of Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid? It’s my favorite movie of all time and I love it—despite all the flaws due to its insane production. What if James Aubrey—the Smiling Cobra—had kept his filthy hands off of it? I wish we got to see Sam’s total vision.
[removed]

Have you seen the TV show Peacemaker? It's a spin off tv show about John Cena's character from The Suicide Squad. The James Gunn sequel to the shitty one with Jared Leto. Cena does a great job with the drama and comedy aspects of the character. I hope he continues to take on more dramatic roles. Ditto for The Rock. He's been cashing checks playing the same character over and over, but after Black Adam bombed, he might think audiences are tired of his shtick. Could give him the motivation to branch out.

Jean Vigo died at 29 with only four films to his name, one of which was his only feature L'Atalante.  It's one of the greatest films ever made and a cornerstone of French poetic realism.  Vigo would have certainly had a career *at least as* esteemed as Jean Renoir, and his influence on the French New Wave was also notable.

I’m sorry but is John Cazale really that big of a what if? He was a good, maybe even very good actor, but he was not like a James Dean level talent. It’s not like he made the movies he was in what they were. They would have probably still been highly acclaimed if other actors were in his roles. 

I’m sure he would have a had a really nice career if he lived longer, but that’s about it.

In my mind it’s the fact that during the first 20 years of ‘moving pictures’, a majority of the people behind the cameras were woman, directors, screenwriters, producers, all other trades. Between 1895 and up to the middle of the 1910’s. Than the movie industry moved from Europe and the east coast (NJ, NY) to California (not only Hollywood, but many other communities tried to build themselves as movie cities), and the bankers got involved, since it was obvious that there were big bucks to make in this industry. Within a decade, moviemaking became a male-dominated, and soon man-exclusive business, and all the women, past and present were pushed out, their contributions erased. The only place for women from that point on were as “stars”, subject to male-approved roles.
The Rock and John Cena are not the kind of people who make great or even good actors. It goes beyond technique. You need vulnerability for acting and that’s the antithesis of who these guys are.

What if David Lynch had gotten the funding to make a film version of Franz Kafka's "Metamorphosis"?

One of the masters of surrealism retelling one of the most bizzare and insightful stories ever written? Easily could have been a masterpiece

Not the biggest, but my own personal choice is what if they paid Robert Duvall for Godfather 3? The original story was supposed to be Michael and Tom Hagen go to war with each other, but they didn't want to give Duvall the same pay as Pacino, so Duvall walked away and  we got what we got...
Cena in Peacemaker shows tremendous vulnerability in Peacemaker.

That’s him trying to play vulnerability, not John Cena actually allowing himself to be vulnerable. 

To be a really good actor, you can’t worry about what people think about you. At least not when you’re working. That’s just not at all who John Cena is. He’s got such a carefully cultivated image.
[removed]

*Verna Fields* decided to keep the shark hidden. Spielberg wanted to show as much of it as possible because of how hard he worked to film it.

absolutely missing is Sergio Leone Leningrad Siege movie.

I don’t know how much I’ll pay to be able  to go back in time and give him some more lifetime. 

In 1986 he was about to get the authorization to shoot in Russia the film about siege of Leningrado which lasted from 8 september 1941 until 27 gennaio 1944.

Here you can find more info: it’s italian but you can get a rough translation with the instruments.

 https://www.ilcineocchio.it/cinema/dossier-il-film-sullassedio-di-leningrado-di-sergio-leone/

I still maintain that we got Kubrick's Napoleon, albeit under a different name.

Barry Lyndon is the story of a provincial outcast who rises to the top of mainstream imperial society through his military exploits, enters into a complicated marriage with a society beauty and then experiences a lonely downfall.

Sound familiar?

I have 2 sort of connected ones.

The American by Aleksei Balabanov - about a Russian and an American who have to flee to one another countries to  go into hiding (the most basic synopsis) - was meant to start Michael Biehn at one point, i remember seeing Mike Tyson mentioned in some of the research - Brother and Brother 2 are up in mg top 10 so seeing that film would've been amazing.

On the topic of Brother, the lead and good friend of Balabanov Sergey Bodrov jr was directing his second feature after Sisters. An actually pretty interesting film and promising for sure. He, his crew of 27 and 93 other people died in a rock-ice slide in [2002](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolka%E2%80%93Karmadon_rock_ice_slide). I would've loved to have seen that film of course, but also the future work of Bodrov and Balabanov.

Another thing with that - apparently Balabanov was in such guilt and grief over the death of Bodrov he was pretty inconsolable for years and it took his producer to get him out of his rutt - he had blamed himself as he told Bodrov and his Cinematographer about the location

It’s not that they need to branch out. They need to stop thinking they’re actually good. They need to get to an actor’s studio and hire a private acting coach. They’re bad community theatre actors. They need to study, and train, read books! They need to embarrass themselves in class trying to do Cherry Orchard or Long Days Journey, Streetcar, and truly take it all in when everyone is cringing. The same is true for Dave Bautista. Peter Dinklage. They’re bad actors. With Marilyn Monroe you saw her with Lee, you saw her reading books, she was devoted and studying. Hillary Swank hired an acting coach before Boys Don’t Cry and Million Dollar Baby. It’s not just about branching out. Dwayne Johnson needs an acting coach by his side 24/7 because he’s awful. So does John Cena.
A little similar, that the Beatles were originally meant to play the vultures in the jungle book
[removed]

>and PJ pulling a rabbit out of a hat, not the ideal vision the two had worked on for years.

I think that's a bit of a stretch. Could he have used a few more months in preproduction? Sure. Anyone would.

But I've seen no indication he's less than happy with the resulting films.
[removed]

What if The Night of the Hunter had been the success it deserved? Charles Laughton wished to pursue a directorial career full time, with a fascinating The Naked and the Dead adaptation in the pipeline, before having his chances obliterated when his debut flopped. 

What if The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes, Billy Wilder's self professed magnum opus, hadn't been butchered by the studio?

> Iirc Coppola didn’t want to direct the Godfather.

Godfather Part 2. He talks about it in [this interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SKY6SDDtRKA).

PJ doesn't shit on the movie because it's in bad taste.  But I'm sure if you get him behind closed doors he'll clearly recognize that short comings of the Hobbit compared to LOTR and how they were all tired to lake of proper pre-production.

Filmmakers HAD been very open about the shortcomings of some of their films: even years after the fact, Jackson seems very pleased with all six films. I don't see a reason to suspect he's being less than truthful.
Very glad brad pitt didn't get his mitts on Wolf of Wall Street

The Beatles had an idea about making The Lord Of The Rings. They wanted to star in it - Lennon would play Gollum, Paul McCartney would play Frodo, George Harrison would be Gandalf and Ringo Starr would play Sam - and they approached Stanley Kubrick to direct. They also wanted to supply the music for it. Kubrick turned it down, saying it was unfilmable and Tolkien also turned them down so the idea died. All things considered it's probably for the best but you've got to wonder what it would have been like to see John Lennon as Gollum...
I always wonder what the Mulholland Drive TV show would've been like.

What if Victor Erice got to film The South as he intended. In the original script, the first half of the movie takes plave in the north of Spain, and the second half is the main character visiting the south, Sevilla I think, to find about her family and her father’s past. Apparently production was shut down, no more money, so the film is only the first half of the story, and a few scenes implying that second half, never filmed. The movie is a masterpiece as it is, but who knows…

I don't think that was really a possibility. In a lot of ways he was his own enemy, he had trouble finishing things, he would often spend endless days editing because he was such a perfectionist. Movies only got released, when they were taken away from him (ambersons, Touch of Evil) or when the money ran out (Othello, Trial, Chimes). 

With proper funding, he could have noodled around with editing a movie for years.

Terry Gilliam was offered Watchmen, but he thought the only way to do it justice was to make a mini series instead of a movie. I think he was right, and what we got instead is forgettable, despite many people saying the ending of the film is better than the ending in the comic, which I think is nonsense, but probably a debate for another thread.
I wish they had made it with German speaking actors , somewhat like the russian film of Faust by  Aleksandr Sokurov. Though that one was dubbed in post I think.
Sergio Leone turned down The Godfather

thank you for the reminder that I'm massively overdue for a barry lyndon rewatch, it's the pinnacle of background set design and warddrobe imo. And has an almost phantom aura that is created when you watch it, effectively absorbing you into another dimension. I'm waxing a bit but I genuinely can't place a memory of when I watch it, I just get sucked in and end up rewatching it every few years to get q sense of that imagination again.

Everyone here has really great ones, so I won’t repeat them, but three I always wanted to see Ralph Bakshi’s sequel to Wizards, Aang Lee’s Hulk 2,  and Wakowski’s Speed Racer 2, both from what I understand had some level of development before scrapped 

But my biggest what if is David lynch full control over the Dune movie, I love Jodowrosky movies but to have it both surreal and weird but close ish to the books I think David lynch was the best shot we’ve had

I still think what we got for watchmen was cool for what it's worth, some of the scenes were really well done and stuck with me, particularly the time scene of dr manhattens perspective and the fidelity and set design, it really has a unique take on comic book movie in that frame by frame the shots really breathe in a unique way.
You and Terry are both right
Probably like twin peaks

This might not be a great answer since it really never even came close to getting off the ground but in the late 60s the Beatles approached Stanley Kubrick to make a Lord of the Rings film. Paul would be Frodo, George as Gandalf, Ringo as Sam and John wanted to play Gollum. I'm almost positive it would have been a disaster but if anyone could have pulled it off its Stanley, who declined because he said LotR was "unfilmable" (which was definitely true at the time). I think Tolkien himself also blocked it so even if everyone was on board it wouldn't have gotten made. But I think it is the movie I would most want to watch out of every failed/unrealized movie in history lol.
Yeah there’s another world where he had Final Cut privilege on every h f and we only got to see like 4 of his films.
Night of the Hunter is one of my next movies!
I think it would've been much better considering the subject matter is a lot more pointed. But hey, I guess we will never know. The film we did get is amazing and I'm thankful we got it 🙏🏽

This is the second time you named Dinklage without anyone calling you out or you providing any kind of defense.

Considering he's regarded by most to be a good actor, I'm wondering if you're mixing him up with someone else.

And if not, what is your critique of his acting?
I didnt know the brotherly dispute detail, that wouldve been something.

If Carl Fukunaga had been able to carry out his vision for the new It movies.

The It movies were terrible, especially the second one. I just wish Fukunaga had been allowed to go ahead with his original vision of the book. To be fair, IIRC, Fukunaga wanted to include the infamous orgy scene from the book and the studio wouldn't go along with it – but what would have happened if he wasn't so willing to die on that hill?

He’s horrible. I want you to go watch Thunder Force right now and tell me he’s a good actor. He’s awful! He did a few years at a random college in New Hampshire. I don’t care about his shtick. He can’t act. It’s wooden and affected.
I mean I can cite Marlon Brando performances that blow, the fact that your citation is a film I forgot existed that was critically reviled doesn't a compelling argument make.

For every Island of Dr Moreau, there’s a Last Tango in Paris, a Godfather, a Streetcar. Do I like On The Waterfront? No. But I respect it. Do I like Don Juan Demarco? No, and I don’t respect it. Brando had a hard time memorizing lines and it got worse over the years. Was his personal life tumultuous? Yes. But he turned in a lot of great things.

For me it has to be what if the people selecting movies for the 12th Venice International Film Festival didn't incorrectly assume that a lot of Japanese family dramas were too Japanese for western audiences. This film festival was, as I understand it, how the west was first introduced to Japanese films. They decided against screening Ozu's work because it was seen as too Japanese for western audiences. So this is where Kurosawa had is breaking through in the west as a result. His work has such a massive impact on New Hollywood as a result. It would be  interesting to go back and see how history would have played out of instead of Samurai movies like Rashomon and Ugetsu they instead screen films like Late Spring instead.

Seeing as how Fukanaga has been accused by multiple people of having a predilection for grooming young girls/women, lets be thankful he didn’t get a chance to do IT — which makes his hard line for the orgy scene particularly disturbing

Will also say that while Fukanaga had strong breakout moments (SIN NOMBRE, TRUE DETECTIVE), his later work was pretty sloppy. SPECTRE is borderline unwatchable.

The one thing that the Watchmen movie absolutely nailed was the opening credits. Easily the best thing Snyder has ever put to film, fantastic visual storytelling,  and a great example of using something unique to film to help tell a story and explore themes (just like the original comic did for comics).

The rest of the movie totally misses the mark when it comes to how it compares to the comic, but for one brief sequence near the stat of the movie, it pulls it off.
[removed]

I agree with you about Faye Dunaway. She is easily one of the best actresses of all-time. 

I believe Jessica Tandy was simply pregnant and unable to do the film version of Streetcar Named Desire.

> The same is true for Dave Bautista. Peter Dinklage. They’re bad actors. With Marilyn Monroe you saw her with Lee, you saw her reading books, she was devoted and studying. 


I can't speak to the others, but Dave Bautista did hire an acting coach, and is pretty famously vocal in his admiration of the craft in pretty much every interview I've seen of him:

> “I’m obsessed with it,” Bautista says of acting. “It’s this puzzle that I can’t figure out. You don’t know if it’s right, but sometimes it feels right. I don’t get those moments a lot, but every once in a while I do. And fuck, to me, there’s nothing like it. It’s a natural high. It’s an addiction.” 

And here's M. Night Shyalaman's opinion on directing Bautista:

> “It felt more like working with Haley [Joel Osment] in Sixth Sense than anything else... When Haley came on set, the set would become reverential—even though he was 10, he was approaching it with an importance, all of his cells were going toward the emotion of his character. Dave conveyed that same thing. **All the other actors fed off his purity of intention. It was infectious in the best way.**”

Or Rian Johnson:

> “I keep telling all my filmmaker friends,” he says, “that **someone is going to give Dave a real dramatic lead role in a movie, and they’re going to look like a genius.**” 


I think he says it himself the best though. And to be honest, I'm not sure how you can read his statement below and come away with the impression that he's anything but genuine towards his work.

>  “Honestly, I could give a fuck [about being a movie star],” he says. “I don't live a great big glamorous life. I live here in Tampa. I don't care about the spotlight, I don't care about fame. **I just want to be a better actor. I want respect from my peers. I don’t need accolades—I really don’t, man. It’s about the experience, about knowing that I accomplished something.**”
I had no idea about the grooming part. That changes things, especially considering his desire to do the orgy scene.

Not the biggest by any means, but one that I think about often is the Sacha Baron Cohen version of Bohemian Rhapsody. Apparently he worked on it for close to a decade and was going to portray a very intense and true to life version of Freddie Mercury with lots of gay stuff, lots of him dealing with aids and a much darker tone. The surviving members of Queen stepped in and shut down his ideas because they wanted a feel good romp to cement their legacy further. Cohen was understandably pissed and washed his hands of the whole project after spending so much time preparing it. I think it’s a shame we got a movie that is so much less than it could have been, even if it was well received.
This is a good point. I have read that a great deal of his Napoleon research went directly into Barry Lyndon
An acting coach is someone who helps you make decisions for a role and someone who might be on set with you. It’s not the same thing as training in a class and really learning craft.
Nah dude, Cena’s a good actor.

As a child I literally thought they WERE the Beatles, because of the character design. Still one of my favorite animated movies.

Jodo's *Dune*

Del Toro's *Hobbit* (this one hurts the most)

Similarly, Sadao Yamanaka directed two masterpieces before being drafted and dying at 28. He was born only a year before Akira Kurosawa and easily could've as great or better if he had only lived.
In a similar way, I think Oppenheimer is close to what Nolan might have done with a Howard Hughes biopic.

Not the biggest 'What If', but the first that came to mind: If Satoshi Kon hadn't passed away at 46, I think he would have had an even larger impact on animated film and would have eventually found a large and receptive audience in the west. Paprika had the feeling of a director just beginning to hit his stride.

> Reservoir Dogs got made because Laurence Bender got the script to Harvey Keitel through a friend of his acting teacher’s wife.

On that subject, the story goes that Quentin Tarantino wanted to cast James Woods as Mr. Orange, but Woods' agent threw the script away when he received it. It wasn't until a couple years later that Woods met Tarantino at a party, where he told him that he wish he could have been in it. Once he learned that Tarantino did, in fact, want to cast him, he immediately fired his agent.
Really Thunder Force? You think that’s a fair movie to judge Dinklage’s entire career. Not the six season Tv show where he won multiple Emmy’s and consistently got critical acclaim.
Jackson is fairly open that the entire Hobbit trilogy had horrendous productions. There wasn't even a storyboard.

A production being *difficult*, is not the same as a movie being disappointing. There are interviews of Jackson as late as 2017, years after the production, where Jackson makes it clear that he's very proud of what he achieved, and rightly so.
Oh wow that’s wild, I hadn’t heard that before. I’d have fired him too lmao

John Carpenter’s Escape From Earth. It would wrap his Snake Plissken trilogy and I’m guessing would have been a Mad Max kinda hybrid. 

I’m not interested in the remake direction. Anybody who’s ever tried has failed. 

It would be nice to read his script for the third movie. I wonder if it ever leaked anywhere?
I honestly think that would've been too distracting to have all three of them, especially Clint. Glad it didn't happen.
Blomkamp being a clueless hack of a director probably extinguishes most of the intrigue around the “what if” here.

I genuinely feel cheated that I live in the universe where Soderbergh didn't direct Moneyball.

I just imagine the interstitial parts of The Laundromat where Gary Oldman and Antonio Banderas explain what a shell corporation is except instead they're explaining how to calculate VORP. And Demetri Martin was supposed to play the Jonah Hill character?!

Like the one flaw of the movie is that they shy away from the statistics & probabilities aspect (because it's too hard to make an audience think about numbers, I guess) and turn it into a 'human story.' Soderbergh has just enough style to make that kind of thing work.

And, of course, in this parallel reality, Soderbergh directing Moneyball frees Magic Mike to be directed by Nicolas Winding Refn.

He always reminded me of Erich von Stroheim in that sense. He had the talent and ability to create masterpieces but not the financial sense that needs to go with them for his projects to be successfully finished.

The Time Burton, Kevin Smith, and Nicholas Cage Superman film, 'Superman Lives'. 

Cancelled 3 weeks before filming started. It was being made by prime Burton, with fucking Nicholas Cage as Superman. That shit would have been so camp and amazing.

>many people saying the ending of the film is better than the ending in the comic, which I think is nonsense, but probably a debate for another thread.

Yeah, those people are missing the whole point of the squid.
I seem to recall reading reports of how miserable he was on the set. There was a ton of studio interference, and the left hand didn’t know what the right was doing.

He can be proud that he achieved what he did with what he had. I would also argue that a leader shouldn’t shift blame, and he had to consider how other people that worked on the film feel. So I can see why anyone wouldn’t openly trash their own work (some obviously still do).

That can all be true and he can still acknowledge that the production of those films was a giant mess.
Del toro directing At The Mountains of Madness too.

[Orson Welles tried to make a Batman movie in the 40s. ](https://www.tonybarrell.com/the-lost-batman-masterpiece/)

"A script was written and the baddies were cast: James Cagney would play the Riddler, Basil Rathbone was the Joker, and Catwoman would be played by Marlene Dietrich.

Humphrey Bogart turned down the role of Two-Face, which went to George Raft. But when Welles insisted that he play Batman himself – in addition to the superhero’s secret alter ego, Bruce Wayne – the Hollywood studio expressed their disapproval, suggesting that Gregory Peck wear the cape and cowl instead. At this point, a petulant Welles called a halt to the whole project."

"del toro" doing whatever he announces he is going to do
